findings.claim: Meta-analysis of survey data estimated ~2% of scientists admit fabricating/falsifying data at least once.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Meta-analysis yielded a pooled weighted estimate of 1.97% (95%CI: 0.86–4.45), with significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q = 61.7777, df = 6, P<0.0001).
findings.evidence: First meta-analysis of misconduct surveys; ~2% admit outright data fabrication/falsification, up to ~34% admit other QRPs.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Meta-analysis yielded a pooled weighted estimate of 1.97% (95%CI: 0.86–4.45), with significant heterogeneity (Cochran's Q = 61.7777, df = 6, P<0.0001).

findings.claim: Text-mining shows p-hacking is widespread across disciplines but its effect on meta-analytic consensus appears weak.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We found significant evidential value in every discipline represented in our text-mining data, irrespective of whether we tested the p-values from the Results or Abstracts (Table 1; Table 2).
findings.evidence: Concludes p-hacking is common but does not drastically alter consensus from meta-analyses; in tension with strong-distortion claims.
findings.effect_size: p-hacking widespread but weak effect on consensus

findings.claim: Statistical power in behavioural sciences has not improved in over 50 years despite repeated calls, consistent with incentives selecting for bad methods.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We show that despite over 50 years of reviews of low statistical power and its consequences, there has been no detectable increase.
findings.evidence: Argues incentives for publication cause natural selection of poor methods; replication slows but does not stop deterioration.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We show that despite over 50 years of reviews of low statistical power and its consequences, there has been no detectable increase.

findings.claim: The Journal Impact Factor is explicitly used in review/promotion/tenure documents, far more at research-intensive institutions.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The percentage was higher for R-type institutions (40%) than for either M-type (18%) or B-type (0%) institutions (Table 2).
findings.evidence: 23% of institutions mentioned JIF; use concentrated in research-intensive universities and overwhelmingly supportive.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The percentage was higher for R-type institutions (40%) than for either M-type (18%) or B-type (0%) institutions (Table 2).

findings.claim: Traditional publication-count criteria dominate biomedical promotion/tenure guidelines while open-science criteria are rare.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Thirty two (35%) institutions had at least one mention of a specific number of peer reviewed publications.
findings.evidence: Peer-reviewed publications mentioned in 95% of guidelines; data sharing in 1%, open-access publishing/registration in none.
findings.effect_size: 35% require a specific number of publications; data sharing mentioned by 1%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Thirty two (35%) institutions had at least one mention of a specific number of peer reviewed publications.

findings.claim: Even under strong public-data-archiving mandates, most archived ecology/evolution datasets are incomplete or unusable for reuse.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In most studies (56%), the archived datasets were incomplete, either because of missing data or insufficient metadata, resulting in a completeness score of 3 or less (Figs 1 and 2A).
findings.evidence: Mandates raise accessibility but not quality; 64% archived in a way that partially or fully prevented reuse.
findings.effect_size: 56% incomplete; 64% archived in a way preventing reuse
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In most studies (56%), the archived datasets were incomplete, either because of missing data or insufficient metadata, resulting in a completeness score of 3 or less (Figs 1 and 2A).

findings.claim: Cross-national survey: nearly all researchers admit using at least one QRP, but frequency (prevalence) is much lower than involvement.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Ninety-four per cent admitted that they had used at least one of these QRPs, and the mean self-reported rate across all QRP items was 42%, with rates for the individual QRPs ranging from 17% to 57%.
findings.evidence: Distinguishes 'use at least once' from frequency; involvement widespread but not systematic use of specific QRPs.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Ninety-four per cent admitted that they had used at least one of these QRPs, and the mean self-reported rate across all QRP items was 42%, with rates for the individual QRPs ranging from 17% to 57%.

findings.claim: When 73 teams analysed the same data and hypothesis, numerical results diverged enormously, revealing hidden analytic uncertainty.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Little more than half the reported estimates were statistically not significantly different from zero at 95% CI, while a quarter were significantly different and negative, and 16.9% were statistically significant and positive.
findings.evidence: Many-analysts design; >95% of variance in results unexplained even after coding all decisions.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Little more than half the reported estimates were statistically not significantly different from zero at 95% CI, while a quarter were significantly different and negative, and 16.9% were statistically significant and positive.

findings.claim: Image-duplication analysis of >20,000 papers found several percent contained inappropriately duplicated images, many suggestive of deliberate manipulation.
findings.claim_source_sentence: A systematic analysis of more than 20,000 articles published between 1995 and 2014 reported that 3.8% of these articles contained inappropriately duplicated images, with at least half of these cases suggestive of deliberate manipulation (24).
findings.evidence: Sets baseline fraud rate; argues paper-mill/broker entities enable fraud growing faster than legitimate science.
findings.effect_size: 3.8% with duplicated images; >=half suggestive of deliberate manipulation
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: A systematic analysis of more than 20,000 articles published between 1995 and 2014 reported that 3.8% of these articles contained inappropriately duplicated images, with at least half of these cases suggestive of deliberate manipulation (24).

findings.claim: Despite policy support, a large share of scientists do not make their data available, reflecting weak individual incentives.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In a study among 1,329 scientists, 46% reported they do not make their data electronically available to others [5].
findings.evidence: Develops a six-category model of data sharing; concludes better incentives are needed as data is not a knowledge commons.
findings.effect_size: 46% do not make data electronically available
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In a study among 1,329 scientists, 46% reported they do not make their data electronically available to others [5].

findings.claim: Registered reports increase the chance that null findings get published, addressing publication bias for early-career researchers.
findings.claim_source_sentence: RRs can thereby increase the chances of publishing null findings, as we demonstrate in 'Benefit 1: Greater faith in research'.
findings.evidence: Exploratory analysis: null findings substantially more likely to be published via open registered reports than conventional routes.
findings.effect_size: qualitative: RRs increase publication of null findings

findings.claim: About a fifth of surveyed scientists implicitly associate questionable research practices with academic success.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Our main finding is that a considerable fraction of about a fifth of researchers associate success with problematic research practices, while only a small minority connect FFP and success.
findings.evidence: Implicit-association evidence that QRPs are perceived as career-advancing, unlike outright misconduct.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Our main finding is that a considerable fraction of about a fifth of researchers associate success with problematic research practices, while only a small minority connect FFP and success.

findings.claim: Some QRPs (e.g., HARKing, selective publication) may under some conditions have neutral or even net-positive effects, complicating the harm narrative.
findings.claim_source_sentence: a growing theoretical and empirical literature suggests that under specific conditions, practices such as HARKing and selectively publishing results may have a neutral or even net positive impact on research progress (Rubin, 2017; de Winter & Happee, 2013).
findings.evidence: Builds a principled QRP taxonomy; most-reported QRPs are selection of analyses/citations/covariates, i.e., omissions.

findings.claim: A systematic replication project could only repeat a fraction of planned preclinical cancer experiments due to missing data and non-reproducible reporting.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The initial goal was to repeat 193 experiments from 53 high-impact papers published between 2010 and 2012, but the obstacles we encountered at every phase of the research lifecycle meant that we were only able to repeat 50 experiments from 23 papers.
findings.evidence: Data needed for power analyses publicly accessible for only 4 of 193 experiments; original authors unresponsive for 32%.
findings.effect_size: 50 of 193 experiments (from 23 of 53 papers) could be repeated
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The initial goal was to repeat 193 experiments from 53 high-impact papers published between 2010 and 2012, but the obstacles we encountered at every phase of the research lifecycle meant that we were only able to repeat 50 experiments from 23 papers.

findings.claim: A survey of researchers across six fields in Portuguese universities documents self-admitted QRPs and their perceived seriousness.
findings.claim_source_sentence: From the n = 9002 researchers contacted, we received n = 1573 responses, for a response rate of 17.4%.
findings.evidence: QRPs widespread across fields/seniority; younger, more prolific researchers and those dismissing seriousness admit more.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: From the n = 9002 researchers contacted, we received n = 1573 responses, for a response rate of 17.4%.

findings.claim: Modelling implies most published research findings are more likely false than true, driven by low power, bias and flexibility.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.
findings.evidence: Foundational metascience argument linking bias/flexibility/financial interest to false findings.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

findings.claim: An incentivised survey of >2,000 psychologists found QRP self-admission rates so high that some practices may be the prevailing norm.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This finding suggests that some questionable practices may constitute the prevailing research norm.
findings.evidence: Truth-telling incentives raised admissions, especially for less-defensible practices; QRPs may be normative.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Combining three different estimation methods, we found that the percentage of respondents who have engaged in questionable practices was surprisingly high.

findings.claim: Reward systems that prize quantity and novelty over quality and reliability are a structural driver of biomedical research waste.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Finally, reward systems incentivise quantity more than quality, and novelty more than reliability.
findings.evidence: Part of the Lancet 'increasing value, reducing waste' series; explicitly indicts scientific reward systems.

findings.claim: Global biomedical research investment reached US$240 billion in 2010, yet much yields little worthwhile output, partly from avoidable waste in priority-setting.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The increase in annual global investment in biomedical research--reaching US$240 billion in 2010--has resulted in important health dividends for patients and the public.
findings.evidence: Quantifies the scale of biomedical R&D spend against which waste estimates are set.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The increase in annual global investment in biomedical research--reaching US$240 billion in 2010--has resulted in important health dividends for patients and the public.

findings.claim: Because full study information is usually inaccessible, billions in research investment are wasted and bias is introduced.
findings.claim_source_sentence: When full information about studies is inaccessible, billions of dollars in investment are wasted, bias is introduced, and research and care of patients are detrimentally affected.
findings.evidence: Calls for institutions and funders to reward investigators who fully disseminate protocols, reports and datasets.
findings.effect_size: journal reports available for only half of all studies
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: However, protocols, full study reports, and participant-level datasets are rarely available, and journal reports are available for only half of all studies and are plagued by selective reporting of methods and results.

findings.claim: Disproportionate research regulation and inefficient management are additional, avoidable sources of biomedical research waste.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Obtaining regulatory and governance approval has become increasingly burdensome and disproportionate to the conceivable risks to research participants.
findings.evidence: Fourth of the Lancet waste series; recommends proportionate regulation and integrating research into practice.

findings.claim: Trial and systematic-review output vastly outpaces capacity to synthesise it, with many redundant or unneeded studies.
findings.claim_source_sentence: There are now 75 trials, and 11 systematic reviews of trials, per day and a plateau in growth has not yet been reached.
findings.evidence: Argues unnecessary trials must be reduced and reviews prioritised to avoid waste.
findings.effect_size: 75 trials and 11 systematic reviews per day
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: There are now 75 trials, and 11 systematic reviews of trials, per day and a plateau in growth has not yet been reached.

findings.claim: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are mass-produced far faster than primary research, many redundant, misleading, or conflicted.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Annual publications between 1991 and 2014 increased 2,728% for systematic reviews and 2,635% for meta-analyses versus only 153% for all PubMed-indexed items.
findings.evidence: 185 antidepressant meta-analyses in 2007-2014; most reviews judged unnecessary, misleading, or conflicted.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Annual publications between 1991 and 2014 increased 2,728% for systematic reviews and 2,635% for meta-analyses versus only 153% for all PubMed-indexed items.

findings.claim: A manifesto proposes optimising methods, reporting, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives to make science more reliable.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Here we argue for the adoption of measures to optimize key elements of the scientific process: methods, reporting and dissemination, reproducibility, evaluation and incentives.
findings.evidence: Influential reform agenda; evidence for effectiveness described as partial and requiring iterative evaluation.

findings.claim: Preregistration separates prediction from postdiction and is proposed to raise the credibility of research findings.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Preregistration distinguishes analyses and outcomes that result from predictions from those that result from postdictions.
findings.evidence: Argues widespread preregistration will sharpen the hypothesis-generation vs testing distinction.

findings.claim: Publishing incentives that reward novel positive results inflate false effects; reforms must make accuracy compete with publishability.
findings.claim_source_sentence: When incentives favor novelty over replication, false results persist in the literature unchallenged, reducing efficiency in knowledge accumulation.
findings.evidence: Restructuring-incentives proposal; a journal of negative results is argued to be an inadequate fix.

findings.claim: Over ~50 years academic incentives have become perverse via funding competition, quantitative metrics and hypercompetition, risking integrity.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Over the last 50 years, we argue that incentives for academic scientists have become increasingly perverse in terms of competition for research funding, development of quantitative metrics to measure performance, and a changing business model for higher education itself.
findings.evidence: Warns a tipping point of untrustworthy science is possible; calls to de-emphasize output.

findings.claim: Expert consensus holds the current faculty incentive/reward system is misaligned with societal needs and the reproducibility crisis.
findings.claim_source_sentence: A burgeoning number of scientific leaders believe the current system of faculty incentives and rewards is misaligned with the needs of society and disconnected from the evidence about the causes of the reproducibility crisis and suboptimal quality of the scientific publication record.
findings.evidence: 22-member panel derived six principles for assessing scientists to realign incentives.

findings.claim: The Hong Kong Principles propose rewarding researchers for integrity behaviours (open science, transparent reporting) rather than output.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Assessment of researchers still rarely includes considerations related to trustworthiness, rigor, and transparency.
findings.evidence: Five principles to drive research improvement by rewarding integrity-strengthening behaviours.

findings.claim: Open research practices are associated with career benefits including more citations, media attention, collaborators and funding.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We review literature demonstrating that open research is associated with increases in citations, media attention, potential collaborators, job opportunities and funding opportunities.
findings.evidence: Argues open practices reward individual researchers, countering fears that sharing harms careers.

findings.claim: Metric-based evaluation (authorship, h-index, JIF) has turned science into a gameable scoring contest that harms early-career scholars.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This has resulted in the incentive structure of science increasingly mimicking economic principles, but rather than a monetary gain, the incentive is a higher score.
findings.evidence: Calls for changing incentive systems to reward quality and transparency.

findings.claim: Citation counts and journal impact factors are weak, sometimes negative predictors of research quality, undermining their evaluative use.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Both citation counts and impact factors were weak and inconsistent predictors of research quality, so defined, and sometimes negatively related to quality.
findings.evidence: Large-scale evidence that high-stakes metrics do not track statistical accuracy, evidential value, or replicability.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Both citation counts and impact factors were weak and inconsistent predictors of research quality, so defined, and sometimes negatively related to quality.

findings.claim: Systematic multi-site replication projects revealed surprising failures to replicate many published psychology findings.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Systematic and multi-site replication projects assessed current understandings and observed surprising failures to replicate many published findings.
findings.evidence: Documents disincentives to conduct replications and framing of replication as personal attack.

findings.claim: Mis-specified random effects mean psychology results generalise far less than assumed, inflating false-positive rates.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Ignoring these constraints can dramatically inflate false-positive rates, and often leads researchers to draw sweeping verbal generalizations that lack a meaningful connection to the statistical quantities they are putatively based on.
findings.evidence: Locates the 'generalizability crisis' as a root cause of the replication crisis.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Ignoring these constraints can dramatically inflate false-positive rates, and often leads researchers to draw sweeping verbal generalizations that lack a meaningful connection to the statistical quantities they are putatively based on.

findings.claim: Review/promotion/tenure processes have increasingly valued research over teaching/service and rely on venue prestige shortcuts.
findings.claim_source_sentence: For instance, over the last few decades, RPT processes have generally increased the value placed on research, at the expense of teaching and service, which often results in an incongruity between how faculty actually spend their time vs. what is considered in their evaluation.
findings.evidence: Documents reliance on impact factor/venue prestige rather than per-item quality in evaluation.

findings.claim: A ten-country Central/Eastern European survey found a favorable research environment and ethics training predict research integrity.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Moreover, seniority and ethics training were identified as predictors of adherence to the principles of research integrity.
findings.evidence: Latent-variable model links favorable research environment to lower misconduct incidence.

findings.claim: Publication and reporting biases and QRPs are prevalent across neuroimaging, animal, preclinical, clinical and genetics literatures.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Recent systematic reviews and empirical evaluations of the cognitive sciences literature suggest that publication and other reporting biases are prevalent across diverse domains of cognitive science.
findings.evidence: Surveys detection methods and emerging solutions for reporting bias across preclinical and clinical domains.

findings.claim: TOP guidelines are poorly adopted in health psychology / behavioural medicine journal policies; preregistration and code-citation standards are adopted least.
findings.claim_source_sentence: TOP guidelines have to-date been poorly adopted within health psychology and behavioural medicine journal policies.
findings.evidence: Cross-sectional rating of 19 journals; standards for reporting guidelines and data transparency adopted most, preregistration and code citation least.
findings.effect_size: journal TOP scores ranged 1 to 13 (median 6) out of 29

findings.claim: Most journal editors support the TOP guidelines but do not treat implementation as a priority; time, resources and authority are barriers.
findings.claim_source_sentence: However, 74% (60/81) did not see TOP as a high priority compared with other editorial tasks, 65% (51/79) do not receive positive recognition from colleagues who are important to them when changing journal policies, and 58% (47/81) did not intend to implement TOP in the next year.
findings.evidence: Theory-based survey of 88 editors; 71% support adopting TOP yet most deprioritise it, revealing an attitude-behaviour gap.
findings.effect_size: 74% did not see TOP as high priority; 58% did not intend to implement within a year
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: However, 74% (60/81) did not see TOP as a high priority compared with other editorial tasks, 65% (51/79) do not receive positive recognition from colleagues who are important to them when changing journal policies, and 58% (47/81) did not intend to implement TOP in the next year.

findings.claim: The TOP Factor was created as an open-science alternative to the Journal Impact Factor; over 5000 signatories and ~1100 journals have adopted TOP standards, most often data citation.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Designed as an alternative to the Journal Impact Factor for evaluating journal quality, the TOP Factor is a quantitative metric that assesses the degree to which journal policies promote transparency and openness.
findings.evidence: Develops the TRUST rating instruments to compute the TOP Factor for journal policies, procedures and practices.
findings.effect_size: over 5000 signatories; ~1100 journals adopting one or more TOP standards
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: At the time of writing, the TOP Guidelines have over 5000 signatories, and 1100 journals have agreed to implement one or more of these standards, most often by specifying data citation standards (seefor a list of such journals).

findings.claim: Only 14% of articles in top orthopaedic journals included a data-sharing statement, and few contacted authors were willing to share data.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Of the 1,084 reviewed articles, only 14% included a DSS.
findings.evidence: Documents low uptake of data-sharing statements and low author willingness to share, arguing for TOP-based mandates.
findings.effect_size: 14% had a data-sharing statement; 22/115 (19.1%) authors responded, 12 (54.5%) willing to share
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Of the 115 emails sent to corresponding authors, only 22 (19.1%) yielded responses, and of those who responded, only 12 (54.5%) expressed a willingness to share their data.

findings.claim: Introducing open-data badges at Psychological Science sharply increased data sharing, while comparison journals without badges stayed near 2-3%.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Across the four comparison journals, for the half years prior to 2014, an average of 3.3% of articles reported open data (range = 1.6% to 4.9%), and after January 1, 2014, the average was 2.1% (range = 1.8% to 2.3%).
findings.evidence: Badges raised reported open data from <3% to 39%; badge-earned data were also more likely to be actually available and usable.
findings.effect_size: comparison journals ~2-3% open data vs Psychological Science rising to 39%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Across the four comparison journals, for the half years prior to 2014, an average of 3.3% of articles reported open data (range = 1.6% to 4.9%), and after January 1, 2014, the average was 2.1% (range = 1.8% to 2.3%).

findings.claim: A Delphi consensus produced a transparency checklist to document the transparency of social and behavioural research reports.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We present a consensus-based checklist to improve and document the transparency of research reports in social and behavioural research.
findings.evidence: Consensus reform tool; adoption/effectiveness not yet empirically demonstrated.

findings.claim: Journal submission guidelines encouraging the 'new statistics' and open practices increased confidence-interval use and open data/materials at Psychological Science.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In Psychological Science, the use of confidence intervals increased markedly overall, from 28% of articles in 2013 to 70% in 2015, as did the availability of open data (3 to 39%) and open materials (7 to 31%).
findings.evidence: Comparison journal changed less; supports journal-level guidelines as a lever for open practices.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In Psychological Science, the use of confidence intervals increased markedly overall, from 28% of articles in 2013 to 70% in 2015, as did the availability of open data (3 to 39%) and open materials (7 to 31%).

findings.claim: The MDAR minimum-reporting framework for the life sciences was piloted; most authors and editors found the accompanying checklist helpful.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Eighty percent of 211 corresponding authors who responded, and 84% of 33 editorial staff, found the checklist “very” or “somewhat” helpful.
findings.evidence: Cross-publisher framework operationalising TOP at article level; pilot on 289 manuscripts, checklist median completion 15 min.
findings.effect_size: 80% of authors and 84% of editors found the MDAR checklist helpful
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Eighty percent of 211 corresponding authors who responded, and 84% of 33 editorial staff, found the checklist “very” or “somewhat” helpful.

findings.claim: Proposes three reforms to reduce bias in medical research: mandatory interest declarations, registered reports, and public study documentation via a WHO repository.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Null findings are more likely to be published through registered reports than traditional formats and registered reports are cited just as often as conventional papers.
findings.evidence: Critical overview arguing registered reports curtail HARKing/p-hacking and spin.

findings.claim: A systematic mapping review identified 187 open-research initiatives in psychology (30 procedural, 70 structural, 87 community-based).
findings.claim_source_sentence: The total number of initiatives included for the review was 187.
findings.evidence: Maps the proliferation of grassroots and structural open-science initiatives; efficacy not evaluated.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: This systematic mapping review identified 187 international initiatives that aim to enhance awareness and uptake of open research practices in psychology, with each categorized into procedural (= 30), structural (= 70) and community-based change (= 87).

findings.claim: In a replication of 100 psychology studies, only 36% of replications were statistically significant vs 97% of originals, and replication effects were half the size.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Thirty-six percent of replications had statistically significant results; 47% of original effect sizes were in the 95% confidence interval of the replication effect size; 39% of effects were subjectively rated to have replicated the original result; and if no bias in original results is assumed, combining original and replication results left 68% with statistically significant effects.
findings.evidence: Landmark large-scale replication defining the 'replication crisis'.
findings.effect_size: 36% of replications significant vs 97% of originals; replication effects half the magnitude
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Ninety-seven percent of original studies had statistically significant results.

findings.claim: The Psychological Science Accelerator is a standing distributed laboratory network enabling large, diverse crowdsourced studies to improve reliability and generalizability.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The Psychological Science Accelerator (PSA) is a distributed network of laboratories designed to enable and support crowdsourced research projects.
findings.evidence: Infrastructure response to low power/nonrepresentative samples; ongoing (not time-limited).

findings.claim: Modelling a scientific community suggests that publishing potentially non-replicable studies and replicating only those of interest can maximize efficiency of knowledge gain.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We find that the publication of potentially non-replicable studies minimizes cost and maximizes efficiency of knowledge gain for the scientific community under a variety of assumptions.
findings.evidence: Contrarian modelling result: low replicability is not necessarily inefficient if managed; challenges replicate-before-publish reforms.

findings.claim: Modelling shows that unless enough negative results are published, false claims can be canonized as fact; publication bias strongly skews the record.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In that analysis, 37 of 38 positive studies were published as positive results, but only 3 of 24 negative studies were published as negative results.
findings.evidence: Markov model of belief; data-dredging and p-hacking worsen canonization of false facts.
findings.effect_size: negative studies published at ~10% the rate of positive studies
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Thus, negative studies were published at scarcely more than 10% the rate of positive studies.

findings.claim: Median statistical power in cognitive neuroscience/psychology is low (0.12-0.73) with no improvement in half a century, and journal impact factor negatively correlates with power.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Median power to detect small, medium, and large effects was 0.12, 0.44, and 0.73, reflecting no improvement through the past half-century.
findings.evidence: 26,841 statistical records from 3,801 papers; false report probability likely exceeds 50% for the literature.
findings.effect_size: median power 0.12/0.44/0.73; JIF negatively correlated with power; false report probability >50%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Median power to detect small, medium, and large effects was 0.12, 0.44, and 0.73, reflecting no improvement through the past half-century.

findings.claim: Psychology's replication concerns constitute a decades-old 'chronic crisis'; the lack of progress across decades is itself notable.
findings.claim_source_sentence: If a crisis does exists, then it is some kind of 'chronic' crisis, as psychologists have been censuring themselves over replicability for decades.
findings.evidence: Editorial framing the replication debate historically.

findings.claim: Papers from more academically productive US states were more likely to report positive (hypothesis-supporting) results, consistent with publish-or-perish pressures increasing bias.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The probability of papers to support the tested hypothesis increased significantly with the per capita academic productivity of the state of the corresponding author (b = 1.383±0.682, Wald test = 4.108, df = 1, p = 0.043, Odds-Ratio (95%CI) = 3.988(1.047–15.193),).
findings.evidence: Empirical support that competitive environments increase both productivity and bias.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The probability of papers to support the tested hypothesis increased significantly with the per capita academic productivity of the state of the corresponding author (b = 1.383±0.682, Wald test = 4.108, df = 1, p = 0.043, Odds-Ratio (95%CI) = 3.988(1.047–15.193),).

findings.claim: A survey of 807 ecologists and evolutionary biologists found high QRP rates: 64% cherry-picking, 42% p-hacking, 51% HARKing.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Across the two groups, we found 64% of surveyed researchers reported they had at least once failed to report results because they were not statistically significant (cherry picking); 42% had collected more data after inspecting whether results were statistically significant (a form of p hacking) and 51% had reported an unexpected finding as though it had been hypothesised from the start (HARKing).
findings.evidence: QRP rates comparable to psychology, implying reproducibility problems extend to ecology/evolution.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Across the two groups, we found 64% of surveyed researchers reported they had at least once failed to report results because they were not statistically significant (cherry picking); 42% had collected more data after inspecting whether results were statistically significant (a form of p hacking) and 51% had reported an unexpected finding as though it had been hypothesised from the start (HARKing).

findings.claim: Catalogues 34 researcher degrees of freedom across planning, running, analysing and reporting that enable p-hacking; usable as a preregistration-quality checklist.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In this review article, we present an extensive list of 34 degrees of freedom that researchers have in formulating hypotheses, and in designing, running, analyzing, and reporting of psychological research.
findings.evidence: Provides the taxonomy later operationalised to assess preregistration quality.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: In this review article, we present an extensive list of 34 degrees of freedom that researchers have in formulating hypotheses, and in designing, running, analyzing, and reporting of psychological research.

findings.claim: Simulations show even a single p-hacking strategy can raise false-positive rates from ~5% to at least 30%, with combinations far higher.
findings.claim_source_sentence: With regard to the different-hacking strategies, we found that even with a single strategy, false-positive rates can typically be raised to at least 30% from the typical 5% threshold with ‘reasonable effort’, that is, without assuming that researchers automate data mining procedures.
findings.evidence: Compiles 12 p-hacking strategies and quantifies false-positive inflation via simulation.
findings.effect_size: single strategy raises false positives from ~5% to >=30%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: With regard to the different-hacking strategies, we found that even with a single strategy, false-positive rates can typically be raised to at least 30% from the typical 5% threshold with ‘reasonable effort’, that is, without assuming that researchers automate data mining procedures.

findings.claim: 'Spin' - reporting that fails to faithfully reflect findings - is prevalent in the biomedical literature and can mislead readers.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Spin has been defined as a specific intentional or unintentional reporting that fails to faithfully reflect the nature and range of findings and that could affect the impression the results produce in readers.
findings.evidence: Reviews prevalence and effects of spin/misrepresentation, a distortion incentivised by publication pressure.

findings.claim: AI-enabled formulaic single-factor NHANES papers exploded from ~4/yr (2014-2021) to 190 in 2024, raising paper-mill and false-discovery concerns.
findings.claim_source_sentence: An average of 4 papers per annum were published between 2014 and 2021, increasing to 33, 82, and 190 in 2022, 2023, and 2024 (to October 9 only) respectively, with recent formulaic manuscripts targeting a relatively small number of indexed journals with moderate impact factor (averaging 3.6).
findings.evidence: 341 formulaic NHANES papers identified; single-factor designs avoid multiple-comparison correction and enable data dredging.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: An average of 4 papers per annum were published between 2014 and 2021, increasing to 33, 82, and 190 in 2022, 2023, and 2024 (to October 9 only) respectively, with recent formulaic manuscripts targeting a relatively small number of indexed journals with moderate impact factor (averaging 3.6).

findings.claim: Defines HARKing, cherry-picking, p-hacking, fishing and data dredging as questionable research practices that at the extreme amount to misconduct.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This knowledge must become widespread so that researchers and readers understand what approaches to statistical analysis and reporting amount to scientific misconduct.
findings.evidence: Didactic taxonomy of analysis/reporting QRPs.

findings.claim: Comparing 105 preregistrations, structured formats restricted researcher degrees of freedom better than unstructured (large effect), but neither eliminated them; coders agreed on the number of hypotheses only 14% of the time.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Coders agreed on the number of hypotheses in only 14.29% of the scores.
findings.evidence: Preregistration effectiveness depends on format; even structured formats leave residual flexibility.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The difference was large (Cliff’s Delta = 0.49).

findings.claim: Argues that with slight modifications, preregistration and registered reports can make exploratory/discovery research more trustworthy.
findings.claim_source_sentence: I will argue that only slight modifications are needed to harness the potential of preregistration and make exploratory research more trustworthy and useful.
findings.evidence: Extends preregistration logic beyond confirmatory studies.

findings.claim: A large preregistered study found no ego-depletion effect (d=0.22, ns) despite a prior meta-analytic d=0.62, illustrating publication-bias inflation.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Despite these efforts, we found no evidence of ego-depletion: participants in the Depletion Condition did not perform differently from participants in the Control Condition on the outcome task, contrary to the ego-depletion hypothesis.
findings.evidence: Preregistered high-powered null; contrasts with inflated meta-analytic effect.
findings.effect_size: no effect (d = 0.22, ns) vs prior meta-analytic d = 0.62
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: However, contrary to the predictions of the hypothesis, we observed no effect of condition,(198) = 1.46,= .146,= 0.22, with participants in the Depletion Condition (= .39,= .14) even showing slightly better performance than those in the Control Condition (= .36,= .13; see).

findings.claim: A journal's compulsory open-data mandate causally increased its article citations by ~1.5-4x (synthetic control), with spillover to earlier articles.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Specifically, the current-year citations of CIE increased from 0.2 ~ 0.4 to 0.9 ~ 1.0 after the open data policy, which means it increased by around 1.5 ~ 4.0 times.
findings.evidence: Natural experiment on a Chinese economics journal; open data as a reputation/impact lever.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Specifically, the current-year citations of CIE increased from 0.2 ~ 0.4 to 0.9 ~ 1.0 after the open data policy, which means it increased by around 1.5 ~ 4.0 times.

findings.claim: Provides a practical guide for social-science journal editors to adopt open-science policies, since editors have power to mandate practices.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Journal editors have a large amount of power to advance open science in their respective fields by incentivising and mandating open policies and practices at their journals.
findings.evidence: Editor-focused implementation guide; part of the incentives-for-openness toolkit.

findings.claim: Infrastructure and mandates for sharing microscopy/cell-image data are emerging, enabling reuse and new analytic tools.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We are now at the dawn of this revolution: infrastructure is being developed for data standardization, deposition, sharing, and analysis; some journals and funding agencies mandate data deposition; data journals publish high-content microscopy data sets; quantification becomes standard in scientific publications; new analytic tools are being developed and dispatched to the community; and huge data sets are being generated by individual labs and philanthropic initiatives.
findings.evidence: Perspective on data reuse enabled by deposition mandates and data journals.

findings.claim: Meta-review of 75 studies: industry-sponsored drug/device studies more often report favorable efficacy (RR 1.27) and conclusions (RR 1.34), an industry bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.
findings.evidence: Cochrane methodology review; funding-source incentive distorts published conclusions.
findings.effect_size: favorable efficacy RR 1.27 (1.17-1.37); favorable conclusions RR 1.34 (1.19-1.51)
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Industry sponsored studies more often had favorable efficacy results, RR: 1.27 (95% CI: 1.17 to 1.37) (25 papers) (moderate quality evidence), similar harms results RR: 1.37 (95% CI: 0.64 to 2.93) (four papers) (very low quality evidence) and more often favorable conclusions RR: 1.34 (95% CI: 1.19 to 1.51) (29 papers) (low quality evidence) compared with non-industry sponsored studies.

findings.claim: Argues software and data-management errors are pervasive and largely undetected, so any computed scientific result could be wrong.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Here I estimate that any reported scientific result could very well be wrong if data have passed through a computer, and that these errors may remain largely undetected.
findings.evidence: Calls for expanded validation of scientific software; a neglected reliability threat.

findings.claim: Reframes the replication crisis as a 'credibility revolution', citing registered reports (perceived higher quality, more negative results) and structural/community changes.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Empirical evidence has also found that Registered Reports are perceived to be higher in research quality than regular articles, as well as equivalent in creativity and importance, while also allowing to report more negative results, which may provide further incentives for researchers to adopt this format.
findings.evidence: Optimistic synthesis of structural, procedural and community reforms.

findings.claim: The Brazilian Reproducibility Initiative aims to replicate 60-100 experiments across a ~63-lab network, powering replications at 95% to counter effect-size inflation.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The Brazilian Reproducibility Initiative began recruiting collaborators to perform replication experiments in 2018, and currently aims to replicate between 60 and 100 experiments from Brazilian biomedical sciences.
findings.evidence: National-scale multicentre replication using a representative sample rather than highly cited papers.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Sample size was calculated to provide 95% power to detect the original effect in each replication.

findings.claim: A manual audit of 250 psychology articles (2014-2017) found transparency practices far from routine: 2% shared raw data, 0% protocols, 3% preregistered, 14% shared materials.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Over half of the articles were publicly available (154/237, 65%, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [59%, 71%]); however, sharing of research materials (26/183; 14%, 95% CI = [10%, 19%]), study protocols (0/188; 0%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]), raw data (4/188; 2%, 95% CI = [1%, 4%]), and analysis scripts (1/188; 1%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]) was rare.
findings.evidence: Baseline prevalence estimates against which reform progress can be tracked; conflict-of-interest statements in only 39%.
findings.effect_size: raw data shared 2%; protocols 0%; preregistration 3%; materials 14%
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Over half of the articles were publicly available (154/237, 65%, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [59%, 71%]); however, sharing of research materials (26/183; 14%, 95% CI = [10%, 19%]), study protocols (0/188; 0%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]), raw data (4/188; 2%, 95% CI = [1%, 4%]), and analysis scripts (1/188; 1%, 95% CI = [0%, 1%]) was rare.

findings.claim: After the ICMJE data-sharing-statement requirement, 68.6% of trials in JAMA/Lancet/NEJM declared data sharing but only 0.6% actually made deidentified data publicly available - a wide declared-vs-actual gap.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The commitment to data sharing substantially decreases when we consider indicators of actual vs declared data sharing: of 334 articles declaring that they would share data, only 2 IPD sets (0.6%; 95% CI, 0.0%-1.5%) were actually deidentified and publicly available on the journal website.
findings.evidence: Mandating a statement raised declared intent but not actual availability; NIH-funded 89% vs industry 61% declared.
findings.effect_size: 68.6% declared data sharing; only 0.6% actually publicly available
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The commitment to data sharing substantially decreases when we consider indicators of actual vs declared data sharing: of 334 articles declaring that they would share data, only 2 IPD sets (0.6%; 95% CI, 0.0%-1.5%) were actually deidentified and publicly available on the journal website.

findings.claim: A meta-synthesis of 45 studies found researchers withhold data largely because incentives, infrastructure, time and skills for sharing are lacking.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The lack of incentives for sharing research data with regards to academic appointment, promotion, recognition, and rewards need to be addressed.
findings.evidence: Qualitative synthesis linking non-sharing to absent rewards and infrastructure.

findings.claim: Analysis of RPT documents at 129 US/Canada universities found public-facing work is undervalued while traditional outputs and citation metrics dominate evaluation.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Moreover, the documents make significant mention of traditional research outputs and citation-based metrics: however, such outputs and metrics reward faculty work targeted to academics, and often disregard the public dimensions.
findings.evidence: Reward systems privilege academic-facing metrics over public-good dimensions of faculty work.

findings.claim: A survey of 2,222 social scientists found ghost and honorary authorship are frequent, driven partly by misconceptions of authorship criteria, distorting credit-based rankings.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Drawing on data from a survey of 2,222 social scientists from around the globe, we study the prevalence of authorship misconduct in the social sciences.
findings.evidence: Authorship misattribution alters academic rankings used in hiring/tenure; argues for contribution disclosures.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Drawing on data from a survey of 2,222 social scientists from around the globe, we study the prevalence of authorship misconduct in the social sciences.

findings.claim: In the first 18 months under the NIH Data Management and Sharing policy, one in five submitted plans still omitted at least one required element.
findings.claim_source_sentence: A notable 20.7% of DMSPs omitted one or more required elements, indicating a need for improved DMS policy conformance.
findings.evidence: Institutional implementation study of the 2023 NIH DMS policy (NOT-OD-21-013); structured templates outperformed unstructured ones on element-level compliance.
findings.effect_size: 79.3% addressed all required elements; 20.7% omitted at least one
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: 79.3% of submitted DMSPs addressed all NIH-required DMSP elements.
findings.study_system: US academic medical center (NIH grant submissions / DMSPs)

findings.claim: Only a quarter of large pharmaceutical companies fully met a multi-component clinical-trial data-sharing standard.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Only 25% of large pharmaceutical companies fully met the data sharing measure.
findings.evidence: Cross-sectional audit adapting 10 data-sharing guidelines; a ranking tool improved compliance to 33% after feedback.
findings.effect_size: 25% fully met (median score 63%, IQR 58-85%); rose to 33% after ranking tool
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The median company data sharing score was 63% (interquartile range 58-85%).

findings.claim: In COVID-19 RCTs, primary outcomes were inconsistent with registries in about half, and almost none of those disclosed the outcome switch.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Primary outcome(s) reported in trial registries and published reports were inconsistent in 49% (n = 104) of trials; of them, only 15% (n = 16) disclosed outcome switching in the report.
findings.evidence: 251 COVID-19 pharmacological RCT reports assessed; transparency and completeness were poor and did not improve after peer review of preprints.
findings.effect_size: 49% inconsistent primary outcomes; only 15% disclosed the switch
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Primary outcome(s) reported in trial registries and published reports were inconsistent in 49% (n = 104) of trials; of them, only 15% (n = 16) disclosed outcome switching in the report.

findings.claim: Progestogens appeared effective in most meta-analyses but showed no effect once analysis was restricted to pre-registered primary outcomes, an example of P-hacking.
findings.claim_source_sentence: When evaluated in registered double-blind trials with analysis restricted to predefined primary outcomes, progestational agents in pregnancy are ineffective.
findings.evidence: 19/29 meta-analyses concluded progestogens were effective; restricting to the 22 trials with pre-registered primary outcomes eliminated the effect.
findings.effect_size: RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.94-1.07) on pre-registered outcomes; 1/22 trials nominally significant
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: There was no effect of progesterone on primary registered dichotomous outcome RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.94-1.07).
findings.study_system: progestogen pregnancy trials (registered vs all outcomes)

findings.claim: Assuming never-ending growth created an unsustainable hypercompetitive biomedical system that deters talent and degrades work quality.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The long-held but erroneous assumption of never-ending rapid growth in biomedical science has created an unsustainable hypercompetitive system that is discouraging even the most outstanding prospective students from entering our profession--and making it difficult for seasoned investigators to produce their best work.
findings.evidence: Influential analysis by Alberts, Kirschner, Tilghman & Varmus calling for systemic reform of the US biomedical research ecosystem.

findings.claim: Peer review, though central to distributing scholarly credit and prestige, remains poorly understood empirically.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Peer review is embedded in the core of our knowledge generation systems, perceived as a method for establishing quality or scholarly legitimacy for research, while also often distributing academic prestige and standing on individuals.
findings.evidence: Maps major theoretical/empirical gaps (editorial responsibility, reviewer bias, function/quality, social/epistemic impact) and calls for a research discipline studying peer review.

findings.claim: Persistent overuse of the journal impact factor ('impact factor mania') is a tragedy-of-the-commons in which individually rational behavior harms science collectively.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Impact factor mania is a variation of the economic theory known as the "tragedy of the commons," in which scientists act rationally in their own self-interests despite the detrimental consequences of their actions on the overall scientific enterprise.
findings.evidence: Argues impact-factor mania persists because it benefits individual scientists, journals and administrators despite harming the scientific enterprise.

findings.claim: Across 20,571 RCTs (1990-2015), only 5.7% used adequate methods and inadequate methods rose, indicating incentives fail to reward rigor.
findings.claim_source_sentence: 5.7% of RCTs used adequate methods (N=1173).
findings.evidence: Meta-research on RCTs in Cochrane reviews; industry funding and trial registration predicted adequate methods, whereas NIH funding and university prestige did not.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: the proportion of RCTs using inadequate methods is high (59.3%) and increasing, potentially slowing progress and contributing to the reproducibility crisis.

findings.claim: Empirical CRediT data from RCTs show contributions concentrate in conceptualization and investigation, with few authors credited for software/data roles.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Most authors participated in the study's conceptualization (44.9%) and investigation (48.8%), but only a fraction of the authors participated in software management (7.4%).
findings.evidence: First empirical analysis of CRediT roles in 446 RCTs (4,185 authors) using PLOS author metadata; proposes a CRediT-RCT taxonomy.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Most authors participated in the study's conceptualization (44.9%) and investigation (48.8%), but only a fraction of the authors participated in software management (7.4%).

findings.claim: A shift from authorship to structured contributorship (CRediT/CRO/CAM) is proposed to better recognize and credit diverse research contributions.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Recent efforts to enable better recognition of contributions to scholarship include the development of the Contributor Role Ontology (CRO), which extends the CRediT taxonomy and can be used in information systems for structuring contributions.
findings.evidence: Reviews ethical/social/technical challenges to authorship and introduces the Contributor Attribution Model (CAM) for machine-readable credit.

findings.claim: India's Medical Council made indexed publications mandatory for promotion, incentivizing authorship-order disputes and prompting calls to credit contribution details instead.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The Medical Council of India (MCI) has made research publications in indexed medical journals an obligatory requirement for promotion of medical teachers.
findings.evidence: Argues authorship-sequence-based credit is arbitrary and that CRediT-style contribution statements should determine merit.

findings.claim: In five CONSORT-endorsing high-impact journals, 87% of trials misreported outcomes, yet journals published only 40% of real-time correction letters.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Fifty-eight trials had discrepancies requiring a correction letter (87%, journal range 67-100%).
findings.evidence: COMPare prospectively checked every outcome against protocols/registries; documented undeclared outcome-switching and journal resistance to corrections.
findings.effect_size: 87% of trials misreported; only 40% (23/58) of correction letters published; mean 5.4 undeclared outcomes/trial
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Twenty-three letters were published (40%) with extensive variation between journals (range 0-100%).
findings.study_system: 67 trials in 5 high-impact journals (NEJM, Lancet, JAMA, BMJ, Ann Intern Med)

findings.claim: When corrected for outcome misreporting, trialists often defended practices contradicting CONSORT, including undermining trial registries.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Trialists frequently expressed views that contradicted the CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) guidelines or made inaccurate statements about correct outcome reporting.
findings.evidence: Qualitative analysis of trialists' published responses to COMPare correction letters; recurring defensive themes including ad hominem and appeals to trust over guidelines.

findings.claim: Many trials measure surrogate, subjective, or selectively reported outcomes that fail to translate into patient benefit.
findings.claim_source_sentence: However, many trials continue to measure and report outcomes that fall short of this clear requirement.
findings.evidence: Reviews outcome problems (surrogate/composite/subjective endpoints, publication and reporting biases, multiplicity, lack of core outcome sets) undermining translation.

findings.claim: Fewer than 2% of cardiovascular papers provide enough materials, data, and analysis scripts to fully reproduce their studies.
findings.claim_source_sentence: We identified that fewer than 2% of cardiovascular research publications provide sufficient resources (materials, methods, data, and analysis scripts) to fully reproduce their studies.
findings.evidence: Screened 639 articles (393 empirical) from Circulation, EHJ and JACC; accessibility varied by study type and journal; calls for journal/funder mandates.
findings.effect_size: <2% fully reproducible; accessibility score 0.08 (case series) to 0.39 (trials)
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: we also showed that the level of accessibility varies across study types with a score of 0.08 for case studies or case series and 0.39 for clinical trials (p = 5.500E-5)

findings.claim: Preregistered psychology studies did not show fewer positive results or smaller effects than matched non-preregistered studies, though they had larger samples and more power analyses.
findings.claim_source_sentence: In contrast to our theoretical expectations and prior research, we did not find that preregistered studies had a lower proportion of positive results (Hypothesis 1), smaller effect sizes (Hypothesis 2), or fewer statistical errors (Hypothesis 3) than non-preregistered studies.
findings.evidence: Compared 193 prize/badge preregistered studies to 193 matched non-preregistered studies; preregistration improved power and impact but not positive-result rate.
findings.effect_size: no reduction in positive-result rate, effect size, or errors; more power analyses and larger N
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Supporting our Hypotheses 4 and 5, we found that preregistered studies more often contained power analyses and typically had larger sample sizes than non-preregistered studies.

findings.claim: Over half of preclinical research is estimated irreproducible, costing about US$28 billion per year in the US alone.
findings.claim_source_sentence: An analysis of past studies indicates that the cumulative (total) prevalence of irreproducible preclinical research exceeds 50%, resulting in approximately US$28,000,000,000 (US$28B)/year spent on preclinical research that is not reproducible-in the United States alone.
findings.evidence: Widely cited economic estimate framing the reproducibility crisis as a large, quantifiable form of research waste.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: An analysis of past studies indicates that the cumulative (total) prevalence of irreproducible preclinical research exceeds 50%, resulting in approximately US$28,000,000,000 (US$28B)/year spent on preclinical research that is not reproducible-in the United States alone.

findings.claim: Ioannidis and colleagues argue current publication practices give a distorted view of scientific reality.
findings.claim_source_sentence: John Ioannidis and colleagues argue that the current system of publication in biomedical research provides a distorted view of the reality of scientific data.
findings.evidence: Essay linking selective publication and reward structures to a biased scientific record.

findings.claim: A 50-year co-citation analysis of QRP research finds systemic factors in how research is conducted are consistently blamed, with attention shifting toward open-science remedies.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Statistical reporting and statistical power emerged as key areas of research, where systemic-level factors in how research is conducted are consistently raised as the precipitating factors for QRPs.
findings.evidence: Document co-citation analysis of 341 QRP papers over 50 years; pre-registration/registered reports dominate remedies while data sharing is under-studied.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The analysis was conducted on a sample of 341 documents that covered the past 50 years of research in QRPs.

findings.claim: Rigorously trialing partial randomisation (lotteries) of research funding is often less feasible and more costly than it appears, favouring alternative evaluation designs.
findings.claim_source_sentence: For many choices of target outcome, RCTs may be less practical and more expensive than they at first appear (in large part due to issues pertaining to sample size and statistical power).
findings.evidence: Metascience analysis of how to evaluate funding-lottery interventions; highlights the interdependence of outcomes, sample size and power.

findings.claim: Wellcome's Institutional Fund for Research Culture became its first scheme to allocate funding by partial randomisation (a funding lottery) among near-equal applications.
findings.claim_source_sentence: IFRC is the first ever Wellcome-funding scheme to use partial randomisation to allocate funding.
findings.evidence: Case study of a real funder adopting a partial lottery: 'Gold' funded directly, 'Silver' funded by randomiser, 'Bronze' not funded; Python randomiser script published.
findings.effect_size: up to £1m grants; Silver-tier applications funded by randomiser
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: It is a departure from Wellcome's previous methods of institutional funding, providing institutions with up to £1m of grant funding to take on ambitious projects that advance research cultures and research environments that are equitable, diverse and supportive.

findings.claim: Because replication is costly and resources finite, the authors offer a framework for deciding which findings to replicate and how, including preregistration.
findings.claim_source_sentence: While replication is rightly considered an indispensable tool of science, financial resources and researchers' time are quite limited.
findings.evidence: Multi-author perspective (incl. Ioannidis, Errington) framing replication as a resource-allocation decision under the reproducibility reforms.

findings.claim: Turning preregistration into a quality signal (e.g., badges) risks stripping it of its intended methodological benefits.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Klonsky's overarching concern is that when preregistration ceases to be a tool for research and becomes an indicator of quality itself (a primary example being preregistration badges), it loses its intended benefits.
findings.evidence: Reply defending preregistration while acknowledging that mandates and badge-style rewards can distort its function.

findings.claim: A novelty-consistency-transparency 'trilemma' may drive opportunistic 'virtue-signalling' use of open-science practices rather than genuine transparency.
findings.claim_source_sentence: While the open science movement grows in importance, the pressure of the trilemma may encourage an opportunistic use of open science practices as a form of virtue signalling compensating for low transparency.
findings.evidence: Argues transparency conflicts with prized novelty and statistical consistency, so incentives can reward performative rather than substantive openness.

findings.claim: Open-science practices in psychology PhD theses (2018-2022) increased only modestly, with no difference between departments with more vs less established open-science support.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Our findings revealed a modest increase of OS over time but no significant difference between departments with more or less-established OS practices.
findings.evidence: Coded 379 studies from 91 theses at two German-speaking psychology departments plus a survey of former PhD students; attitudes mattered more than local norms.
findings.effect_size: modest increase 2018-2022; no significant department difference
findings.study_system: 379 studies in 91 psychology PhD theses (2 departments)

findings.claim: An empirical review concludes that using journal rank (impact factor) to assess research is bad scientific practice, tied to unreliability and retractions.
findings.claim_source_sentence: These data corroborate previous hypotheses: using journal rank as an assessment tool is bad scientific practice.
findings.evidence: Reviews data linking journal rank to citations, methodological soundness, expert ratings and retractions; argues any rank (not just Impact Factor) has this effect.

findings.claim: Fanelli argues the 'reproducibility crisis' narrative is largely mistaken, disputing claims that most published results are unreliable.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This article provides an overview of recent evidence suggesting that this narrative is mistaken, and argues that a narrative of epochal changes and empowerment of scientists would be more accurate, inspiring, and compelling.
findings.evidence: Contrarian meta-scientific opinion pushing back on the crisis framing that motivates many open-science reforms.

findings.claim: A cross-disciplinary meta-assessment found publication biases overall small, and high publication/citation rates were NOT associated with greater bias, though misconduct and early-career status were.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Authors publishing at high rates and receiving many citations were, overall, not at greater risk of bias.
findings.evidence: Probed bias patterns in a large random sample of meta-analyses across all disciplines; small/early/highly cited studies overestimated effects, misconduct and small collaborations predicted inflation.
findings.effect_size: biases overall small; high-output authors not at greater risk; misconduct and early-career linked to inflated effects
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: The magnitude of these biases varied widely across fields and was overall relatively small.
findings.study_system: random sample of meta-analyses across all disciplines

findings.claim: Academic publishing serves two often-misaligned goals (knowledge dissemination and credentialing), letting commercial publishers extract large profits while pressuring scholars to maximize publication metrics.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Commercial publishing companies have capitalized on the centrality of publishing to the scientific enterprises of knowledge dissemination and academic recognition to extract large profits from academia by leveraging unpaid services from reviewers, creating financial barriers to research dissemination, and imposing substantial fees for open access.
findings.evidence: Perspective/analysis paper on misaligned incentives in academic publishing and journal reform.

findings.claim: A multi-actor qualitative study found stakeholders agreed research climates harm integrity yet felt unable to change them, revealing a circle of blame among actor groups.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Even though all participants agreed that current research climates need to be addressed, participants generally did not feel responsible nor capable of initiating change.
findings.evidence: Semi-structured interviews and focus groups with diverse research-system actors in the Flemish biomedical landscape.

findings.claim: Interviewees said current research assessments overvalue outputs while ignoring the processes essential to research quality and integrity, and called for valuing quality over quantity.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Interviewees noted that current research assessments overvalued outputs but largely ignored the processes deemed essential for research quality and integrity.
findings.evidence: Companion multi-actor qualitative study on how success in science is defined and assessed.

findings.claim: Argues that, despite being derided, rigorous field-adjusted centralized quantitative metrics could improve research practices, defending metrics against qualitative-only assessment.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Although often derided, quantitative metrics could help improve research practices if they are rigorous, field-adjusted, and centralized.
findings.evidence: Perspective defending quantitative metrics in researcher assessment.

findings.claim: A review plus two-round Delphi survey identified 10 DORA-compliant measures of research quality and impact, a more explicit set than prior efforts.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Our work contributes to the field by identifying 10 DORA-compliant measures of research quality and impact, a more comprehensive and explicit set of measures than prior efforts.
findings.evidence: Literature review and Delphi survey of researchers and research leaders in biomedical institutions.
findings.effect_size: 10 DORA-compliant measures identified; 44 panelists round one
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: Rating of measures by 44 panelists (60%) in Round One and 24 (55%) in Round Two of a Delphi survey resulted in consensus on the high importance of 5 measures: research advances existing knowledge, research plan is innovative, an independent body of research (or fundamental role) supported by peer-reviewed research funding, research outputs relevant to discipline, and quality of the content of publications.

findings.claim: Argues global university rankings, like GDP for economies, drive universities to 'grow' up rankings rather than thrive, and are incompatible with socially responsible practice.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Draws parallels between the problematic use of GDP to evaluate economic success with the use of global university rankings to evaluate university success.
findings.evidence: Perspective on responsible metrics and global university rankings.

findings.claim: Introduces the Relative Citation Ratio, an article-level field-normalized citation metric offered as an alternative to the invalid use of journal impact factors to identify influential papers.
findings.claim_source_sentence: The resulting Relative Citation Ratio is article level and field independent and provides an alternative to the invalid practice of using journal impact factors to identify influential papers.
findings.evidence: Bibliometric method development and validation using NIH-authored articles.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: To illustrate one application of our method, we analyzed 88,835 articles published between 2003 and 2010 and found that the National Institutes of Health awardees who authored those papers occupy relatively stable positions of influence across all disciplines.

findings.claim: Synthesizing five years of research, argues four urgent actions are needed to foster better research, including realigning assessments to value elements that strengthen science.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Here, we translate our findings in four actions that are urgently needed to foster better research.
findings.evidence: Synthesis of a five-year research program on research integrity and assessment.

findings.claim: A survey of 338 US/Canada faculty found they describe 'quality', 'prestige', and 'impact' of journals in overlapping, ill-defined ways, undermining evaluation regimes built on these terms.
findings.claim_source_sentence: While relying on self-reported definitions that are not linked to their behavior, this study's findings highlight that faculty often describe these distinct terms in overlapping ways.
findings.evidence: Survey of faculty across US and Canadian institutions on journal evaluation terms.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: We address this question by surveying 338 faculty members from 55 different institutions in the U.S. and Canada.

findings.claim: A consensus view recommends research funders adopt a Research Integrity Promotion Plan built around 6 core topics to strengthen integrity policy.
findings.claim_source_sentence: This Consensus View offers a range of examples of how funders are already promoting research integrity, distills 6 core topics that funders should cover in a RIPP, and provides guidelines on how to develop and implement a RIPP.
findings.evidence: Multi-organization consensus recommendations for research funders.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: This Consensus View offers a range of examples of how funders are already promoting research integrity, distills 6 core topics that funders should cover in a RIPP, and provides guidelines on how to develop and implement a RIPP.

findings.claim: The SCOPE framework provides a structured five-stage process to bridge the gap between responsible-research-assessment principles and their practical implementation.

findings.evidence: Framework paper with four case studies of responsible research assessment.
findings.effect_size_source_sentence: SCOPE bridges the gap between principles and their implementation by providing a structured five-stage framework by which evaluations can be designed and implemented, as well as evaluated.

findings.claim: A co-creative Delphi with researchers, managers and funders produced consensus recommendations addressing how Open Research's resource intensity, APC costs, and reward practices undermine its equity aims.
findings.claim_source_sentence: Using a co-creative modified Delphi method, we generated consensus-driven recommendations that address three key problem areas: the resource-intensive nature of Open Research, the high cost of article processing charges, and obstructive reward and recognition practices at funders and research institutions that undermine the implementation of Open Research.
findings.evidence: Co-creative modified Delphi with a diverse community of stakeholders.
